references.text: Jesus says that a prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and among his own household – a parallel to Luke's formulation that no prophet is welcome in his home town.
Mark's parallel account where Jesus states the same principle: "A prophet is not despised anywhere except in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own house."
John recounts the same proverb that a prophet is not honored in his own homeland, confirming that this was a well-known saying of Jesus.
Jeremiah is an example of a prophet who was rejected by his own people, illustrating the general principle Jesus speaks about.
Ezekiel was sent to a stubborn and disobedient people – an example of how prophets were often rejected by their own.

Jesus himself expands on this principle in the following verses by referring to Elijah and Elisha, both of whom were sent to Gentiles instead of Israel because prophets were not received by their own.
Stephen accuses the Jews of always resisting the Holy Spirit and persecuting the prophets, confirming the pattern Jesus describes.
Jesus laments over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those sent to the city – an expression of the same principle that God's messengers are rejected by their own people.
"He came to his own, and his own did not receive him" – John's summary of the same principle of rejection that Jesus formulates in Luke 4:24.
